{{short description|Mathematical abstraction of level sets}}
[[File:3D-Leveltorus-Reebgraph.png|thumb|right|300px|Reeb graph of the height function on the torus.]]
A '''Reeb graph'''<ref name="Y. Shinagawa, T.L. Kunii 1991. pp.66-78">Y. Shinagawa, T.L. Kunii, and Y.L. Kergosien, 1991. Surface coding based on Morse theory. IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications, 11(5), pp.66-78</ref> (named after [[Georges Reeb]] by [[René Thom]]) is a [[mathematics|mathematical]] object reflecting the evolution of the [[level sets]] of a real-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]] on a [[differentiable manifold|manifold]].<ref>Harish Doraiswamy, Vijay Natarajan, [http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925772108001193 Efficient algorithms for computing Reeb graphs], Computational Geometry 42 (2009) 606–616</ref> A similar concept was introduced by [[Georgy Adelson-Velsky|G.M. Adelson-Velskii]] and [[Alexander Kronrod|A.S. Kronrod]] and applied to analysis of [[Hilbert's thirteenth problem]].<ref name=Gorban2013>{{cite journal |last1=  Gorban| first1= Alexander N.|year= 2013 |title= Thermodynamic Tree: The Space of Admissible Paths|journal= SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems|volume=12|issue= 1|pages= 246–278|doi= 10.1137/120866919| arxiv= 1201.6315 | s2cid= 5706376}}</ref><ref>G. M. Adelson-Velskii, A. S. Kronrod, About level sets of continuous functions with partial derivatives, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR, 49 (4) (1945), pp. 239–241.</ref> Proposed by G. Reeb as a tool in [[Morse theory]],<ref>G. Reeb, Sur les points singuliers d'une forme de Pfaff complètement intégrable ou d'une fonction numérique, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 222 (1946) 847–849</ref> Reeb graphs are the natural tool to study multivalued functional relationships between 2D scalar fields <math>\psi</math>, <math>\lambda</math>, and <math>\phi</math> arising from the conditions
<math> \nabla \psi = \lambda \nabla \phi </math> and <math>\lambda \neq 0</math>, because these relationships are single-valued when restricted to a region associated with an individual edge of the Reeb graph. This general principle was first used to study [[Neutral density#Spatial dependence|neutral surfaces]] in [[oceanography]].<ref name=Stanley2019>{{cite journal |last1=Stanley |first1=Geoffrey J. |title=Neutral surface topology |journal=Ocean Modelling |date=June 2019 |volume=138 |pages=88–106 |doi=10.1016/j.ocemod.2019.01.008|arxiv=1903.10091 |bibcode=2019OcMod.138...88S |s2cid=85502820 }}</ref>

Reeb graphs have also found a wide variety of applications in [[computational geometry]] and [[computer graphics]],<ref name="Y. Shinagawa, T.L. Kunii 1991. pp.66-78"/><ref>Y. Shinagawa and T.L. == Formal definition ==

Given a [[topological space]] ''X'' and a [[continuous function]] ''f'':&nbsp;''X''&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''', define an [[equivalence relation]] ~ on ''X'' where ''p''~''q'' whenever ''p'' and ''q'' belong to the same [[Connected component (topology)|connected component]] of a single [[level set]] ''f''<sup>&minus;1</sup>(''c'') for some real ''c''. The '''Reeb graph''' is the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] ''X''&nbsp;/~ endowed with the [[quotient topology]].

Generally, this quotient space does not have the structure of a finite graph. Even for a smooth function on a smooth manifold, the Reeb graph can be not one-dimensional and even non-[[Hausdorff space]].<ref name="I. Gelbukh  2024. pp.343-365">I. Gelbukh, 2024. On the topology of the Reeb graph. Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen, 104(3-4), pp.343-365</ref>

In fact, the [[compactness]] of the manifold is crucial: The Reeb graph of a smooth function on a closed manifold  is a one-dimensional [[Peano continuum]] that is [[homotopy equivalence|homotopy equivalent]] to a finite graph.<ref name="I. Gelbukh  2024. pp.343-365">I. Gelbukh, 2024. On the topology of the Reeb graph. Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen, 104(3-4), pp.343-365</ref>
In particular, the Reeb graph of a smooth function on a closed manifold with a finite number of critical values –which is the case of [[Morse function]]s, [[Morse–Bott function]]s or functions with isolated critical points – has the structure of a finite graph.<ref name="O. Saeki  2022. pp.8740-8768">O. Saeki, 2022. Reeb spaces of smooth functions on manifolds. Int. Math. Res. Not., 11, pp.8740-8768</ref>

== Structure of the Reeb graph defined by a smooth function==

Let <math>f:M\to {\mathbb R}</math> be a [[smooth function]] on a [[closed manifold]] <math>M</math>. The structure of the Reeb graph <math>R_f</math> depends both on the manifold <math>M</math> and on the class of the function <math>f</math>.

===The first Betti number of the Reeb graph=== 

Since for a smooth function on a closed manifold, the Reeb graph <math>R_f</math> is one-dimensional,<ref name="I. Gelbukh  2024. pp.343-365">I. Gelbukh, 2024. On the topology of the Reeb graph. Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen, 104(3-4), pp.343-365</ref> we consider only its first [[Betti number]] <math>b_1(R_f)</math>; if <math>R_f</math> has the structure of a finite graph, then <math>b_1(R_f)</math> is the [[circuit rank|cycle rank]] of this graph. An upper bound holds<ref name="I. Gelbukh  2018. pp.843-863">I. Gelbukh, 2018. Loops in Reeb Graphs of n-Manifolds. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 59(4), pp.843-863</ref><ref name="I. Gelbukh  2024. pp.343-365">I. Gelbukh, 2024. On the topology of the Reeb graph. Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen, 104(3-4), pp.343-365</ref> 

<math>b_1(R_f)\le corank(\pi_1(M))</math>, 

where <math>corank(\pi_1(M))</math> is the [[Rank_of_a_group#Generalizations_and_related_notions|co-rank]] of the [[fundamental group]] of the manifold. If <math>\dim M\ge3</math>, this bound is tight even in the class of simple [[Morse function]]s.<ref name="L.P. Michalak  2021. pp.1038-1060">L.P. Michalak, 2021. Combinatorial Modifications of Reeb Graphs and the Realization Problem.  Discrete & Computational Geometry , 65, pp.1038-1060</ref> 

If <math>\dim M=2</math>, for [[smooth function]]s this bound is also tight, and in terms of the [[genus]] <math>g</math> of the surface <math>M^2</math> the bound can be rewritten as
<math display=block>b_1(R_f)\le
   \begin{cases}
     g, & \text{if  }  M^2 \text{  is orientable }\\
     g/2, & \text{if  }  M^2 \text{  is non-orientable }.
   \end{cases}
</math>

If <math>\dim M=2</math>, for [[Morse function]]s, there is a better bound for the cycle rank. Since for  [[Morse function]]s, the Reeb graph <math>R_f</math> is a finite graph,<ref name="O. Saeki  2022. pp.8740-8768">O. Saeki, 2022. Reeb spaces of smooth functions on manifolds. Int. Math. Res. Not., 11, pp.8740-8768</ref> we denote by <math>N_2</math> the number of [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] with [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] 2 in <math>R_f</math>. Then<ref name="L.P. Michalak  2018. pp.749-762">L.P. Michalak, 2018. Realization of a graph as the Reeb graph of a Morse function on a manifold. Topological Methods in Nonlinear Analysis, 52(2), pp.749-762</ref>
<math display=block>b_1(R_f)\le
   \begin{cases}
     g-N_2, & \text{if  }  M^2 \text{  is orientable }\\
     (g-N_2)/2, & \text{if  }  M^2 \text{  is non-orientable }.
   \end{cases}
</math>

===Leaf blocks of the Reeb graph=== 

If <math>f:M\to R</math> is a [[Morse function|Morse]] or [[Morse_theory#Morse–Bott_theory|Morse–Bott  function]] on a [[closed manifold]], then its Reeb graph <math>R_f</math> has the structure of a finite graph.<ref name="O. Saeki  2022. pp.8740-8768">O. Saeki, 2022. Reeb spaces of smooth functions on manifolds. Int. Math. Res. Not., 11, pp.8740-8768</ref> This finite graph has a specific structure, namely
* If <math>f</math> is [[Morse function|Morse]], then <math>R_f</math> has no [[Loop (graph theory)|loop]]s, and all its [[Biconnected component|leaf blocks]] are [[Complete graph|complete graphs]] <math>K_2</math>, i.e.,  closed intervals<ref name="I. Gelbukh  2022. pp.61-77">I. Gelbukh, 2022. Criterion for a graph to admit a good orientation in terms of leaf blocks.  Monatshefte für Mathematik, 198, pp.61-77</ref>
* If <math>f</math> is [[Morse_theory#Morse–Bott_theory|Morse–Bott]], then <math>R_f</math> has no [[Loop (graph theory)|loop]]s, and each its [[Biconnected component|leaf block]] contains a [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertex]] with [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] at most 2<ref name="I. Gelbukh  2022. pp.1-16">I. Gelbukh, 2022. Realization of a Graph as the Reeb Graph of a Morse–Bott or a Round Function.  Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica , 59(1), pp.1-16</ref>

== Description for Morse functions ==

If <math>f</math> is a [[Morse function]] with distinct [[critical value (critical point)|critical value]]s, the Reeb graph can be described more explicitly. Its nodes, or vertices, correspond to the critical level sets <math>f^{-1}(c)</math>. The pattern in which the arcs, or edges, meet at the nodes/vertices reflects the change in topology of the level set <math>f^{-1}(t)</math> as <math>t</math> passes through the critical value <math>c</math>. For example, if <math>c</math> is a minimum or a maximum of <math>f</math>, a component is created or destroyed; consequently, an arc originates or terminates at the corresponding node, which has [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] 1. If <math>c</math> is a [[saddle point]] of index 1 and two components of <math>f^{-1}(t)</math> merge at <math>t = c</math> as <math>t</math> increases, the corresponding vertex of the Reeb graph has degree 3 and looks like the letter "Y". The same reasoning applies if the index of <math>c</math> is <math>dim X-1</math> and a component of <math>f^{-1}(c)</math> splits into two.
